paragraphs: Creating labeled training data often requires expensive expert judgment. This paper studies a cheaper interaction: asking whether two items belong to the same class. A computer uses these pairwise answers to assemble groups, after which experts can assign labels to the groups. The central question is how to minimize the number of comparisons.

The authors analyze two probabilistic models of how classes are formed. In the first, the partition of items into classes is chosen uniformly at random. They characterize algorithms that minimize the average query count and analyze their complexity. In the second, each item independently chooses a class according to a fixed distribution.

For that second model, the authors study a particular algorithm family and compare it with a random strategy. Its average-query optimality remains a conjecture, rather than a proved result. They also propose ways to accommodate incorrect or inconsistent expert answers. The contribution connects annotation cost to explicit mathematical models while distinguishing established optimality from a promising unresolved claim.
neurips-2021-active-clustering-for-label.tldr: Pairwise expert comparisons can support cheaper training-data labeling, with query-optimal clustering algorithms established under one random class model.

paragraphs: Combining several neural networks can improve classification accuracy and the reliability of confidence estimates, but running the whole ensemble costs memory and computation. Distillation attempts to transfer its behavior into one model. This paper investigates why the resulting model can still fall short of the ensemble it learns from.

The authors' central assumption is that successful distillation should preserve the diversity of functions represented by the ensemble members. They empirically find that ordinary distillation transfers this diversity poorly, especially when complex models make almost no training errors. Agreement on training examples can therefore conceal differences in how the models behave elsewhere.

Their solution perturbs inputs to seek cases where ensemble members disagree, then uses those samples during distillation. These examples expose distinctions that the student would otherwise have less opportunity to learn. Experiments show greater diversity in the distilled model and improved performance. The findings support disagreement-seeking inputs as a way to narrow the performance gap, without establishing that distillation completely reproduces the ensemble.
neurips-2021-diversity-matters-when-lear.tldr: Distilling on inputs that expose ensemble disagreement transfers more diversity and empirically improves the resulting single model.

paragraphs: Ensemble methods combine multiple predictions, but combining graphs poses a different problem from combining class labels or numerical estimates. Each prediction contains a structured collection of relationships. This paper studies how to combine such outputs, focusing on abstract meaning representation, or AMR, where a parser represents the meaning of text as a graph.

The authors formulate aggregation as finding the largest graph with the strongest support from a collection of predicted graphs. This turns agreement among models into a graph-mining objective. Finding the optimal solution is NP-hard, so they develop an efficient heuristic that approximates the desired solution rather than claiming to solve the optimization exactly.

Experiments combine predictions from state-of-the-art AMR parsers across five standard benchmark datasets. The combined predictions are more accurate than those of any individual participating model. These results show that useful agreement can be recovered at the level of graph structure. The contribution includes both a formal statement of the aggregation problem and a practical method supported by AMR parsing experiments.
neurips-2021-ensembling-graph-prediction.tldr: A graph-mining heuristic combines AMR parser outputs into predictions that outperform each individual parser on five benchmarks.

paragraphs: In nonconvex optimization, a small gradient can occur near a saddle point even when useful downhill directions remain. This paper develops a gradient-based algorithm for reaching an approximate second-order stationary point of a smooth function. That target requires approximate stationarity together with control of negative curvature; it does not establish a global minimum.

The main technique implements a robust Hessian power method using only gradients. It seeks negative curvature near saddle points without requiring the algorithm to access the Hessian directly. This provides a mechanism for finding escape directions and improves the dimension dependence compared with the perturbed gradient descent methods considered in the paper.

For dimension n and accuracy ε, the stated iteration bound is roughly log(n)/ε^1.75, with additional logarithmic factors suppressed. The improvement concerns powers of log(n), while retaining the ε dependence of the cited faster-accuracy comparison. In the stochastic setting, the bound is roughly log²(n)/ε^4 under the same notation. Numerical experiments support the theoretical results, complementing the analysis of how gradient information can reveal useful curvature.
neurips-2021-escape-saddle-points-by-a-s.tldr: A gradient-only curvature-finding method escapes saddle points with improved logarithmic dependence on problem dimension.

paragraphs: Predicting an agent's movement in an interactive setting requires accounting for other agents. Variational autoencoders are used to represent these systems compactly and generate diverse possible trajectories. This paper asks whether a commonly used formulation actually encodes the history of social interactions in the representation used to predict future movement.

The authors identify a failure mode they call social posterior collapse: the model can ignore historical social context. They argue that this can produce substantial prediction errors and poor generalization, analyze why it happens, and propose measures to address it. Their framework also includes a sparse graph attention message-passing layer, called sparse-GAMP, which helps detect the failure in experiments.

Tests on real-world trajectory datasets confirm that social posterior collapse occurs and that the proposed measures alleviate it. The resulting generalization improvement is specifically reported when past social context contains information useful for prediction. This qualification matters: the contribution concerns making informative interactions count in the model, rather than asserting that social history improves every forecasting situation.
neurips-2021-exploring-social-posterior-.tldr: The paper identifies and mitigates a VAE failure that ignores social history, improving generalization when that history informs trajectory prediction.

paragraphs: Drug discovery models often have too few compounds with measured activities or ADMET properties to learn effective predictions. This paper addresses that shortage by transferring knowledge from earlier assays conducted by different laboratories and against different protein targets. The challenge is to share useful information despite substantial differences between the source and destination tasks.

The proposed FRML method builds its predictor from layers of neural subnetworks called functional regions. All assays share an initial setting of the predictor's weights. A separate region localization network then selects the regions relevant to each assay, allowing the common starting model to be customized rather than transferred identically to every task.

This compositional design is intended to improve generalization across varied tasks, including tasks outside the training distribution. Experiments on virtual screening and ADMET prediction report better performance than the state-of-the-art baselines considered. The method also offers interpretability concerning relationships among assays. Its contribution is a structured way to combine shared learning with task-specific selection when labeled compounds are scarce.
neurips-2021-functionally-regionalized-k.tldr: FRML transfers knowledge between drug discovery assays through shared initialization and assay-specific selection of neural subnetworks.

paragraphs: Learning graph representations can require many rounds of gradient computation and substantial hardware resources. This paper develops a cheaper route based on singular value decomposition, or SVD. The key challenge is that the matrices needed for this route would themselves be expensive to store if constructed explicitly.

For several graph learning tasks, the authors derive first-order approximations to state-of-the-art models and express their training through SVD of an implicitly defined matrix. Their framework performs the decomposition without calculating that matrix's entries. The resulting models have closed-form training solutions, avoiding gradient-based optimization while producing competitive test performance on graphs including citation and biological interaction networks.

The SVD solution can also initialize a deeper network designed to behave linearly on a particular parameter hyperplane and nonlinearly almost everywhere else. After initialization on that hyperplane, the network can be fine-tuned for only a few epochs. Overall, the authors report training hundreds of times faster than state-of-the-art methods while remaining competitive empirically, making computational accessibility a central part of the contribution.
neurips-2021-implicit-svd-for-graph-repr.tldr: Implicit SVD trains approximations to graph learning models without materializing large matrices, achieving competitive results with much faster training.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns a class to each image location, making it a dense prediction problem. Neural networks can learn features in which information about different classes is entangled. The paper highlights how this can produce biased predictions, particularly for under-represented classes whose training examples offer less diversity.

The authors propose a stochastic training scheme that can be applied across model architectures. It first extracts class-specific information from an entangled feature map. At each training iteration, it randomly chooses a class and suppresses information associated with that class through feature selection. The intervention takes place in the learned feature space.

Repeatedly removing selected class information reduces dependencies between class features and encourages more separated, less biased representations. Models trained this way achieve strong results on multiple semantic segmentation benchmarks, with especially notable gains for under-represented classes. The findings support changing the training process as a way to address feature dependence in dense prediction, extending attention beyond the classification settings where such issues have more often been studied.
neurips-2021-learning-debiased-and-disen.tldr: Randomly suppressing class-specific feature information during segmentation training reduces class dependencies and especially improves under-represented classes.

paragraphs: Models that learn compact representations of images, shapes, or audio often need different architectures and training objectives for each signal type. This paper uses neural fields to pursue a common approach across these domains, including audiovisual data. Its model, GEM, aims to capture the structure of a dataset in a low-dimensional manifold.

GEM encourages three properties: coverage of that manifold, locally linear behavior, and preservation of local distances. Together, these constraints organize the representation so nearby portions can support meaningful movement between samples. The authors report that following linear regions produces perceptually consistent interpolations, connecting the geometry of the learned space to changes in the represented signals.

The learned manifold also supports recovering representations from inputs, producing diverse image completions, and generating audio or image signals across modalities. Moving through the manifold can additionally produce new samples in the signal domains. The contribution is a shared representation-learning framework whose geometry supports several operations, rather than requiring a separate modality-specific formulation for each kind of signal.
neurips-2021-learning-signal-agnostic-ma.tldr: GEM learns structured neural-field manifolds across signal types, supporting interpolation, completion, cross-modal generation, and new samples.

paragraphs: A useful prediction interval should cover the true outcome at its promised rate while indicating greater uncertainty where prediction risk is higher. These are different requirements: coverage alone does not ensure that uncertainty varies meaningfully across inputs. This paper develops a lightweight method intended to provide both properties for almost any deep learning model.

The method, LVD, combines ideas from conformal prediction and kernel regression. Its intervals have finite-sample local coverage guarantees without assumptions on the data distribution. Local coverage goes beyond an aggregate marginal guarantee, addressing coverage in a more localized sense. The method also aims to make intervals discriminative, so their uncertainty reflects differences in expected prediction risk.

Across diverse datasets, the authors report that LVD matches or exceeds existing uncertainty methods on measures including coverage rate and prediction accuracy. They also report advantages in scalability and flexibility. The contribution brings a theoretical local coverage property together with an efficient construction, addressing the practical need to add informative uncertainty estimates without extensive changes to the underlying neural network.
neurips-2021-locally-valid-and-discrimin.tldr: LVD combines conformal prediction and kernel regression to provide locally valid prediction intervals that reflect differences in prediction risk.

paragraphs: Language models, translation systems, and tagging models learn different internal representations, but their relationships are not immediately apparent. This paper compares 100 feature spaces drawn from networks trained on language tasks. It adapts an encoder-decoder transfer-learning method from computer vision to investigate how these representations are organized relative to one another.

The analysis reveals a low-dimensional structure linking word embeddings, syntactic and semantic tasks, and future-word embeddings. Representations from language and translation models vary smoothly within this structure. The authors call it a language representation embedding: it describes relationships among feature spaces, rather than simply providing another representation of individual words or sentences.

This embedding predicts how well each feature space maps to human brain responses measured with fMRI during natural-language stimulation. A metric built from its principal dimension also highlights a hierarchy in the brain's language processing. These findings suggest that the embedding captures some aspects of neural language representation. They establish a correspondence, while the authors' interpretation remains appropriately qualified as capturing only part of that structure.
neurips-2021-low-dimensional-structure-i.tldr: Relationships among 100 language feature spaces form a low-dimensional structure that predicts their correspondence with human brain responses.

paragraphs: Generalization theory seeks to explain how well a trained network will perform on new data, yet theoretical bounds often track observed performance poorly. This paper develops bounds that account for the geometry of the network's learned features. It combines classification margins with optimal transport costs calculated between independent random subsets drawn from the training distribution.

The transport cost normalizes the margins, giving them a scale informed by the feature space rather than treating margin size in isolation. The authors interpret this cost as a generalization of variance that captures structural properties of the representation. This links prediction confidence, expressed through margins, to how the learned features are distributed.

The theoretical analysis identifies feature concentration and separation as important factors in generalization. Empirically, the resulting bounds robustly predict generalization error on large-scale datasets using training data and network parameters. The findings support evaluating both the organization of learned features and the margins they produce, helping connect a theoretical account of generalization with patterns observed in trained networks.
neurips-2021-measuring-generalization-wi.tldr: Optimal-transport-normalized margin bounds connect feature geometry to generalization and empirically predict error on large-scale datasets.

paragraphs: Max-k-Cut and correlation clustering are graph partitioning problems for which strong approximation guarantees can come with substantial memory requirements. For Max-k-Cut and the Max-Agree form of correlation clustering, the best guarantees rely on semidefinite programs with numbers of variables and constraints growing quadratically with the number of vertices. This makes large instances difficult to store.

The paper develops polynomial-time algorithms based on Gaussian sampling that nearly match those approximation guarantees. Their memory use grows as O(n + |E|), where n is the number of vertices and |E| is the number of edges. The result trades the large optimization representation for storage proportional to the graph's vertices and edges.

For dense graphs received as a stream, the authors combine their approach with sparsification to remove dependence on the edge count from storage complexity. That additional memory saving comes with a slightly weaker approximation ratio. The contribution therefore provides two explicit quality-versus-storage options, retaining near-best guarantees in the main setting and accepting a modest guarantee reduction for dense streaming inputs.
neurips-2021-memory-efficient-approximat.tldr: Gaussian sampling nearly preserves leading graph-partitioning approximation guarantees with memory proportional to vertices and edges.

paragraphs: Positive-unlabeled learning starts with labeled positive examples and an unlabeled collection containing both positive and negative cases. The task has two connected parts: estimating how much of the unlabeled collection is positive, and using that estimate to train a classifier. This paper addresses difficulties that earlier approaches encounter in high-dimensional data.

The authors introduce Best Bin Estimation, or BBE, for estimating the positive fraction, and Conditional Value Ignoring Risk, or CVIR, as an objective for classifier training. BBE has formal guarantees when a model can cleanly separate a small subset of positive examples. This is a stated sufficient condition for the guarantee, rather than a claim that all positives must be perfectly separated.

Their final algorithm, called (TED)^n, alternates between estimating the mixture proportion and training the classifier. The authors report that both component methods outperform earlier approaches empirically, and that alternation significantly improves both estimates and classification. The contribution treats prevalence estimation and predictive learning as linked procedures that can improve together, with a conditional theoretical foundation for the estimation component.
neurips-2021-mixture-proportion-estimati.tldr: BBE and CVIR jointly improve positive-unlabeled learning, with BBE guarantees when a small positive subset can be cleanly separated.

paragraphs: Multilingual language models can share knowledge across languages, helping languages with limited training resources. This paper argues that models trained only on plain text miss useful linguistic structure shared across languages. It proposes incorporating universal dependency syntax into multilingual pre-training so that grammatical relationships become an explicit part of what the model learns.

The proposed model supports both dependency parsing and language modeling. Universal dependency structure serves two roles: it is a training objective and part of the learned representation. This means syntactic information contributes directly to learning and remains available for downstream use. The authors also present this explicit structure as a source of improved interpretability.

Evaluations cover cross-lingual natural language understanding benchmarks and linguistic structure parsing datasets. The model outperforms multilingual-BERT and XLM-R in the reported comparisons. These findings support the usefulness of combining shared grammatical structure with multilingual language modeling. The contribution is therefore both representational and empirical: syntax is built into the model's learning process, and the resulting approach shows stronger cross-lingual performance in the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2021-multilingual-pre-training-w.tldr: Adding universal dependency syntax to multilingual pre-training improves reported cross-lingual understanding and parsing results.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning a nonlinear dynamical system from a single trajectory, where successive observations are correlated. The system applies an unknown matrix and a known nonlinear link function, then adds unbiased noise. The goal is to estimate the matrix under an expansivity property of the link function.

The authors provide an offline algorithm that does not require the system to be mixing, an assumption used by previous nonlinear results. For mixing systems, they also improve sample complexity. In the one-pass streaming setting, their stochastic gradient method with reverse experience replay matches the offline algorithm's sample complexity when mixing holds.

The expansivity condition has substantive consequences. For the ReLU link, which lacks the required property, the authors show that learning from the dynamical system can require exponentially many samples in the state dimension, despite its tractability with independent samples. Simulations support the analysis and show that naive stochastic gradient descent can be highly suboptimal. The results explain why methods tailored to temporal dependence can outperform standard gradient training.
neurips-2021-near-optimal-offline-and-st.tldr: Algorithms tailored to correlated trajectories improve nonlinear system learning, with offline guarantees beyond mixing and matching streaming rates under mixing.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains a decision-making policy from an existing dataset, avoiding the costs of collecting experience through online trial and error. Many approaches restrict policies to behavior supported by that dataset to improve robustness. This paper examines the accompanying tradeoff: those restrictions can also limit what a learned policy is able to achieve.

The proposed method, Model-based Adaptable Policy Learning, or MAPLE, directly addresses decisions outside the dataset's support. It learns a policy designed to adapt its behavior in those regions when deployed. The central change is therefore in the policy's intended capability: learning includes preparation for deployment situations that are not adequately represented by the offline examples.

Experiments use offline datasets for MuJoCo control tasks. The authors report robust decisions in out-of-support regions and better performance than the state-of-the-art algorithms considered. These results support adaptable policy learning as a way to explore the performance potential constrained by conventional offline restrictions. The evidence concerns the evaluated control settings, rather than a universal guarantee of reliable decisions everywhere beyond the training data.
neurips-2021-offline-model-based-adaptab.tldr: MAPLE learns offline policies that adapt beyond dataset-supported regions and improves performance in reported MuJoCo control experiments.

paragraphs: The effect of a classification loss can depend on how useful information is organized in the data. This paper studies that interaction in an analytically solvable model, comparing quadratic and logistic losses. Its focus is the over-parameterized regime, where models have enough capacity to fit training data while still potentially generalizing well.

Using statistical physics methods, the authors derive precise asymptotic expressions for training and test errors of random feature models. Their data model has an input covariance assembled from independent blocks. This lets them vary both the prominence of low-dimensional structure and how that structure aligns with the target function being learned.

Within this setup, data structure has a greater effect on error curves for logistic loss than for mean-squared loss in the over-parameterized regime. As the task becomes easier, the performance advantage of logistic loss grows. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR10 support these insights. The result connects loss selection to data geometry through a controlled theoretical model, with additional empirical evidence from image classification.
neurips-2021-on-the-interplay-between-da.tldr: A solvable random-feature model shows that useful data structure can favor logistic over quadratic loss, supported by image-classification experiments.

paragraphs: This paper examines Thompson Sampling in combinatorial semi-bandits, focusing on how its performance changes as dimension grows. It measures performance through regret, the accumulated loss relative to a better decision strategy. The central finding is that this algorithm can have unfavorable scaling in a setting where its exploration behavior might otherwise seem appealing.

The theoretical results show exponential dependence of regret on ambient dimension and almost-linear minimax regret. The phenomenon holds across a variety of assumptions in the Bernoulli setting, including both linear and nonlinear reward functions. Thus, within the analyzed problem family, the difficulty is not confined to nonlinear rewards alone.

Adding a fixed amount of forced exploration does not eliminate the problem. Numerical experiments complement the theory by showing very poor practical performance in some high-dimensional situations. Together, these findings establish a substantive weakness for Thompson Sampling in the studied semi-bandit setting. The claim is about demonstrated adverse regimes and scaling behavior, rather than every high-dimensional application or every possible modification of the algorithm.
neurips-2021-on-the-suboptimality-of-tho.tldr: Thompson Sampling can suffer exponentially dimension-dependent regret in combinatorial semi-bandits, even with fixed forced exploration.

paragraphs: A useful three-dimensional scene description needs more than geometry: it should also identify semantic categories and distinguish individual object instances. This paper unifies those requirements into panoptic 3D scene reconstruction from one RGB image. The target is a complete reconstruction within the camera's viewing volume, together with semantic and instance segmentations.

The proposed approach learns to lift two-dimensional image features into a three-dimensional volumetric representation and propagate them through that representation. This connects information extracted from the input image to a scene description that includes shape, category, and instance identity. Treating these outputs together supports a richer form of scene understanding than geometric reconstruction alone.

The authors also introduce an evaluation metric that considers reconstruction quality and panoptic segmentation jointly. Their experiments show better performance than alternative approaches on this combined task. The contribution therefore includes a unified task, a learned reconstruction approach, and an evaluation method aligned with the richer output. Such representations are motivated by applications including robotics, motion planning, and augmented reality.
neurips-2021-panoptic-3d-scene-reconstru.tldr: The method reconstructs 3D geometry, semantic categories, and object instances jointly from a single RGB image.

paragraphs: Training models on encrypted data can help preserve privacy, but it makes ordinary model-development procedures difficult. In particular, choosing hyperparameters through validation is extremely challenging in the encrypted setting. This paper proposes a logistic regression framework designed to avoid that selection process while remaining suitable for homomorphic encryption.

The method transforms logistic regression into a corresponding ridge regression problem for the logit function. This formulation also avoids approximating the sigmoid function. Removing both sigmoid approximation and hyperparameter selection targets two practical complications of encrypted training. The authors support the framework theoretically with a new generalization error bound for encrypted data.

Experiments on several real-world datasets report better classification results and approximately 68% lower latency than previous models. These findings indicate that the reformulation can improve predictive performance and computation time together in the evaluated settings. Here, the parameter-free claim concerns avoiding hyperparameter selection; the resulting classifier still learns a model. The contribution is a training formulation that addresses the particular computational and validation difficulties created by encryption.
neurips-2021-parameter-free-he-friendly-.tldr: An encrypted logistic regression reformulation avoids sigmoid approximation and hyperparameter selection, with better reported accuracy and roughly 68% lower latency.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning must share useful information across clients while accommodating their different, often small datasets. This paper proposes pFedGP, which combines a shared neural-network kernel with a separate Gaussian process classifier for each client. The design addresses a tension: Gaussian processes can work well with little data, but learning a good kernel requires broader evidence.

Sharing the kernel allows clients to contribute to the representation used by their individual classifiers. The authors also introduce two inducing-point extensions. One targets improved generalization when data is scarce, while the other reduces computational cost. A PAC-Bayes analysis provides a generalization bound for new clients, and empirical evaluation shows that the bound gives non-vacuous guarantees.

Experiments cover CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CINIC-10, and an additional setup involving input noise. The authors report well-calibrated predictions and substantial improvements over baseline methods, with accuracy gains reaching up to 21%. That figure is a reported maximum rather than a uniform gain. The results support combining a common learned kernel with local Bayesian classifiers to handle client heterogeneity.
neurips-2021-personalized-federated-lear.tldr: pFedGP shares a learned kernel across clients while personalizing Gaussian process classifiers, improving accuracy and calibration in reported experiments.

paragraphs: A model can fit noisy training data exactly and still make few errors on new examples. This phenomenon, called benign overfitting, challenges the intuition that fitting noise must always destroy generalization. The paper studies it in linear classification, focusing on the maximum margin classifier in an over-parameterized setting.

The analysis assumes that data come from sub-Gaussian mixtures. Within that model, the authors derive a tight bound on the classifier's risk, meaning its prediction error on new data. The bound precisely characterizes conditions under which benign overfitting can occur and improves on previous theoretical results. Its conclusions are therefore tied to a specified distributional setting and classifier.

The findings also have direct implications for over-parameterized logistic regression. Their significance is a sharper account of when interpolation and small test error can coexist in classification. Rather than treating exact training fit as sufficient evidence of either success or failure, the analysis connects generalization to conditions within the data model. The contribution is theoretical clarification of the phenomenon in this linear setting.
neurips-2021-risk-bounds-for-over-parame.tldr: Tight risk bounds characterize when over-parameterized maximum margin classifiers can benignly overfit data from sub-Gaussian mixtures.

paragraphs: Larger neural architectures have helped vision and language systems, yet reinforcement learning commonly uses small multilayer perceptrons. This paper investigates that mismatch in actor-critic methods by replacing small networks with larger architectures containing skip connections and normalization. It tests whether limited data explains the apparent preference for simpler models.

The experiments show that directly substituting larger modern networks can cause unstable training and poor performance. The authors find that dataset size is not the limiting factor in their investigation. Instead, they argue that instability associated with taking gradients through the critic is responsible, directing attention toward the learning dynamics rather than model capacity alone.

Spectral normalization mitigates this instability and enables stable training with larger architectures. Once the networks are smoothed this way, larger models yield significant performance improvements in the reported experiments. The results suggest that architectural improvements offer additional opportunities in reinforcement learning alongside algorithmic changes. They support addressing critic-related instability before concluding that increased network capacity is unhelpful.
neurips-2021-towards-deeper-deep-reinfor.tldr: Spectral normalization stabilizes larger actor-critic networks, allowing increased model capacity to improve reinforcement learning performance.

paragraphs: Many variants of k-means address outliers, poor local solutions, or data poorly described by Euclidean distance. Combining these ideas individually can leave a method without a coherent theoretical foundation. This paper develops a unified framework for robust center-based clustering that supports a broad class of dissimilarity measures.

The framework uses Median-of-Means estimation and includes several popular k-means variants as special cases. The authors derive uniform concentration bounds to complete analyses of these methods, then connect those bounds to the robust framework through Dudley's chaining arguments. This supplies a common mathematical treatment rather than relying solely on separate empirical justifications for each component.

The analysis requires neither assumptions about the distribution of outlying observations nor a prescribed relationship between observation count and feature count. Under mild conditions, it establishes strong consistency and an error rate of O(n^-1/2), improving on the previous results described by the authors. Experiments on real and synthetic datasets support the methods. The theoretical guarantees remain conditional, while allowing substantial flexibility in outlier distributions and dimensionality.
neurips-2021-uniform-concentration-bound.tldr: A Median-of-Means framework unifies robust clustering variants and establishes consistency and O(n^-1/2) error rates under mild conditions.
